putnam-1987-a1.title: Use the complex variable z = x + iy
putnam-1987-a1.body:
Let $z=x+iy$. Then
$$z^2=(x^2-y^2)+2xy\,i,\qquad \frac1z=\frac{x-iy}{x^2+y^2}\quad(z\ne0).$$
So for $(x,y)\ne(0,0)$:
- $(x,y)\in A\iff \mathrm{Re}\left(z^2-\frac1z\right)=x^2-y^2-\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}=0$;
- $(x,y)\in B\iff \mathrm{Im}\left(z^2-\frac1z\right)=2xy+\frac{y}{x^2+y^2}=3$.

The origin is in neither $A$ nor $B$ (the fractions are undefined). Hence
$$A\cap B=\{z\ne0:\ z^2-\tfrac1z=3i\}=\{z\neq0:\ z^3-3iz-1=0\}.$$

On the other hand,
$$z^3-3iz-1=\big(x^3-3xy^2\big)+i\big(3x^2y-y^3\big)-3ix+3y-1=\big(x^3-3xy^2+3y-1\big)+i\big(3x^2y-y^3-3x\big).$$
Its real part vanishes iff $(x,y)\in C$ and its imaginary part vanishes iff $(x,y)\in D$. So $C\cap D=\{z:\ z^3-3iz-1=0\}$. Since $z=0$ is not a root ($-1\ne0$), the two sets coincide:
$$A\cap B=C\cap D.$$
∎

putnam-1987-a2.title: Count digits up to the m-digit numbers
putnam-1987-a2.body:
There are $9\cdot10^{k-1}=10^k-10^{k-1}$ numbers with $k$ digits, contributing $k(10^k-10^{k-1})$ digits. So the number of digits used by all numbers with at most $m$ digits is
$$S(m)=\sum_{k=1}^mk\left(10^k-10^{k-1}\right)=m\,10^m-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}10^k=m\,10^m-\frac{10^m-1}{9}$$
(summation by parts: each $10^k$ with $k<m$ appears with coefficient $k-(k+1)=-1$). Check: $S(1)=9$, $S(2)=189$.

By definition $f(n)=m$ iff $S(m-1)<10^n\le S(m)$. Now
$$S(1984)>1984\cdot10^{1984}-10^{1984}=1983\cdot10^{1984}>10^{1987},$$
$$S(1983)<1983\cdot10^{1983}<10^4\cdot 10^{1983}=10^{1987}.$$
Hence $S(1983)<10^{1987}\le S(1984)$, i.e. $f(1987)=1984$.

**Answer:** $1984$.

putnam-1987-a2.title: Estimate first, then confirm
putnam-1987-a2.body:
Up to the $m$-digit numbers we have used roughly $m\cdot10^m$ digits (precisely $S(m)=m10^m-\frac{10^m-1}9$, between $(m-\frac19)10^m$ and $m10^m$). We want $m\,10^m\approx10^{1987}$, i.e. $m+\log_{10}m\approx1987$. Since $\log_{10}m\approx3.3$ for $m\approx1984$, try $m=1984$: $1984\cdot10^{1984}\approx1.98\cdot10^{1987}$, just above $10^{1987}$, while $m=1983$ gives about $1.98\cdot10^{1986}$, below. The precise bounds in the first approach make this rigorous.

**Answer:** $f(1987)=1984$.

putnam-1987-a3.title: Solve the equation
putnam-1987-a3.body:
**General solution.** Write $f(x)=e^xu(x)$ (any function can be, with $u=e^{-x}f$). Then $f'=e^x(u+u')$, $f''=e^x(u+2u'+u'')$, so
$$f''-2f'+f=e^xu''.$$
The equation becomes $u''=2$, so $u=x^2+ax+b$ for constants $a,b$:
$$f(x)=(x^2+ax+b)e^x,\qquad f'(x)=\big(x^2+(a+2)x+(a+b)\big)e^x .$$

A real quadratic $x^2+px+q$ is positive for all $x$ iff its discriminant is negative, $p^2<4q$ (if $p^2\ge4q$ it has a real root). Since $e^x>0$:
- $f>0$ everywhere $\iff a^2<4b$;
- $f'>0$ everywhere $\iff (a+2)^2<4(a+b)\iff a^2+4<4b$.

**(a) No.** Take $a=0$, $b=\frac12$: $f(x)=(x^2+\frac12)e^x>0$ for all $x$, but $f'(x)=(x^2+2x+\frac12)e^x$ and $f'(-1)=-\frac12e^{-1}<0$.

**(b) Yes.** If $f'>0$ everywhere then $4b>a^2+4>a^2$, so $f>0$ everywhere.

putnam-1987-a3.title: Qualitative argument for (b)
putnam-1987-a3.body:
Using the general solution $f=(x^2+ax+b)e^x$ from the first approach, one can also see (b) directly: as $x\to-\infty$, $f(x)\to0$ (the exponential beats the quadratic). If $f'>0$ everywhere, $f$ is strictly increasing. For any $x$ and any $t<x-1$ we get $f(x-1)>f(t)$; letting $t\to-\infty$ gives $f(x-1)\ge0$, and hence $f(x)>f(x-1)\ge0$.

For (a), positivity of $f$ does not prevent $f$ from decreasing somewhere: the example $f=(x^2+\frac12)e^x$ dips near $x=-1$, since $f'(-1)<0$.

**Answer:** (a) No; (b) Yes.

putnam-1987-a4.title: Identify P as a quadratic form in the differences
putnam-1987-a4.body:
**Structure of $P$.** With $u=1$, $P(x,y,z)=F(y-x,z-x)$, so the hypothesis says $P(ux,uy,uz)=u^2P(x,y,z)$. Writing $P=\sum_kP_k$ as a sum of homogeneous parts, $\sum_ku^kP_k(x,y,z)=u^2\sum_kP_k(x,y,z)$ for all real $u$, so (comparing coefficients of the polynomial in $u$) $P_k=0$ for $k\ne2$: $P$ is a quadratic form. Also $P(x,y,z)=F(y-x,z-x)=P(0,y-x,z-x)$. Let
$$Q(s,t)=P(0,s,t)=\alpha s^2+\beta st+\gamma t^2,$$
a quadratic form, so $P(x,y,z)=Q(y-x,z-x)$ as a polynomial identity (it holds for all real arguments), hence also for complex arguments.

**Coefficients.** $P(0,1,0)=Q(1,0)=\alpha=5$, $P(0,0,1)=Q(0,1)=\gamma=6$, and $P(1,0,0)=Q(-1,-1)=\alpha+\beta+\gamma=4$, so $\beta=-7$:
$$P(x,y,z)=5(y-x)^2-7(y-x)(z-x)+6(z-x)^2 .$$

**The condition.** Let $s=B-A$, $t=C-A$, with $|s|=10$, $s\ne0$. Then $P(A,B,C)=0$ reads
$$6\left(\frac ts\right)^2-7\frac ts+5=0 .$$
Its discriminant $49-120=-71<0$, so the roots $w=\frac{7\pm i\sqrt{71}}{12}$ are complex conjugates, and $|w|^2=w\bar w=\frac56$ (product of the roots). Hence
$$|C-A|=|t|=|s|\sqrt{\tfrac56}=10\sqrt{\tfrac56}=\frac{5\sqrt{30}}3\approx9.13 .$$

**Answer:** $\dfrac{5\sqrt{30}}{3}$.

putnam-1987-a5.title: Stokes' theorem on a surface avoiding the origin
putnam-1987-a5.body:
Such an $\vec F$ does **not** exist. Suppose it did.

**The line integral of $\vec G$.** Let $\gamma$ be the ellipse $x^2+4y^2=1$, $z=0$, parametrized by $\mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\tfrac12\sin t,0)$, $0\le t\le2\pi$. On $\gamma$, $x^2+4y^2=1$, so
$$\vec G\cdot\mathbf r'(t)=(-y)(-\sin t)+x\cdot\tfrac12\cos t=\tfrac12\sin^2t+\tfrac12\cos^2t=\tfrac12 .$$
Since $\vec F=\vec G$ on the plane $z=0$ by (iii), $\displaystyle\oint_\gamma\vec F\cdot d\mathbf r=\int_0^{2\pi}\tfrac12\,dt=\pi .$

**Stokes.** Let $\Sigma$ be the upper half of the ellipsoid $x^2+4y^2+z^2=1$, $z\ge0$. It is a smooth oriented surface whose boundary is $\gamma$, and it does not contain the origin (the origin is not on the ellipsoid), so $\vec F$ is $C^1$ on a neighbourhood of $\Sigma$ by (i). Stokes' theorem and (ii) give
$$\oint_\gamma\vec F\cdot d\mathbf r=\iint_\Sigma(\mathrm{Curl}\,\vec F)\cdot\mathbf n\,dS=0,$$
contradicting $\pi\ne0$. Hence no such $\vec F$ exists. ∎

putnam-1987-a5.title: Conservative fields on a simply connected domain
putnam-1987-a5.body: The domain $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$ is simply connected (every loop can be contracted while avoiding a single point in three dimensions). A $C^1$ curl-free field on a simply connected domain is a gradient, $\vec F=\nabla\phi$, so its integral around every closed curve is $0$. But by (iii) the integral of $\vec F$ around the ellipse $x^2+4y^2=1$ in the plane $z=0$ equals the integral of $\vec G$, which is $\pi$ (computed with $x=\cos t$, $y=\frac12\sin t$; the integrand is $\frac12\,dt$). Contradiction, so no such $\vec F$ exists. ∎

putnam-1987-a6.title: Group the terms by number of digits
putnam-1987-a6.body:
All terms are positive, so we may group them freely. For $k\ge1$ let $B_k$ be the sum of the terms with $3^{k-1}\le n<3^k$, i.e. with exactly $k$ base-3 digits.

**Sum of $x^{a(n)}$ over $k$-digit numbers.** Such an $n$ has leading digit $1$ or $2$ and $k-1$ further digits. The number of them with exactly $j$ zeros is $2\binom{k-1}{j}2^{k-1-j}$, so
$$\sum_{3^{k-1}\le n<3^k}x^{a(n)}=2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\binom{k-1}{j}x^j2^{k-1-j}=2(x+2)^{k-1}.$$

**Bounds.** For these $n$, $27^{k-1}\le n^3<27^k$, hence
$$\frac{2}{27}\left(\frac{x+2}{27}\right)^{k-1}<B_k\le 2\left(\frac{x+2}{27}\right)^{k-1}.$$
So $\sum_n\frac{x^{a(n)}}{n^3}=\sum_kB_k$ converges iff the geometric series $\sum_k\left(\frac{x+2}{27}\right)^{k-1}$ converges, i.e. iff $x+2<27$.

**Answer:** the series converges exactly for $0<x<25$.

putnam-1987-b1.title: Symmetry x ↦ 6 − x
putnam-1987-b1.body:
Call the integral $I$. The substitution $x\mapsto6-x$ maps $[2,4]$ onto itself and swaps $9-x$ and $x+3$, so
$$I=\int_2^4\frac{\sqrt{\ln(x+3)}\,dx}{\sqrt{\ln(x+3)}+\sqrt{\ln(9-x)}} .$$
(The denominator is positive on $[2,4]$ since $x+3\ge5$ and $9-x\ge5$.) Adding the two expressions for $I$,
$$2I=\int_2^4\frac{\sqrt{\ln(9-x)}+\sqrt{\ln(x+3)}}{\sqrt{\ln(9-x)}+\sqrt{\ln(x+3)}}\,dx=\int_2^41\,dx=2 .$$

**Answer:** $I=1$.

putnam-1987-b1.title: Shift to a symmetric interval
putnam-1987-b1.body:
Put $x=3+t$, $t\in[-1,1]$: the integrand becomes $\phi(t)=\dfrac{g(-t)}{g(-t)+g(t)}$ with $g(t)=\sqrt{\ln(6+t)}$. Then $\phi(t)+\phi(-t)=1$, so $\phi-\frac12$ is an odd function and integrates to $0$ over $[-1,1]$. Hence
$$I=\int_{-1}^1\phi(t)\,dt=\int_{-1}^1\tfrac12\,dt=1 .$$

**Answer:** $1$.

putnam-1987-b2.title: Beta integrals
putnam-1987-b2.body:
**Lemma.** For integers $a,b\ge0$, $\displaystyle\int_0^1x^a(1-x)^b\,dx=\frac{a!\,b!}{(a+b+1)!}$. Equivalently, for $0\le j\le t$,
$$\frac1{\binom tj}=(t+1)\int_0^1x^j(1-x)^{t-j}\,dx .$$
*Proof.* Induct on $b$. For $b=0$ the integral is $\frac1{a+1}$. For $b\ge1$, integrating by parts,
$$\int_0^1x^a(1-x)^b\,dx=\Big[\tfrac{x^{a+1}}{a+1}(1-x)^b\Big]_0^1+\frac b{a+1}\int_0^1x^{a+1}(1-x)^{b-1}dx=\frac{b}{a+1}\cdot\frac{(a+1)!(b-1)!}{(a+b+1)!}=\frac{a!\,b!}{(a+b+1)!}.\ \square$$

**Main computation.** By the lemma (all $j=r+k\le r+s\le t$),
$$\sum_{k=0}^s\frac{\binom sk}{\binom t{r+k}}=(t+1)\int_0^1\sum_{k=0}^s\binom skx^{r+k}(1-x)^{t-r-k}dx=(t+1)\int_0^1x^r(1-x)^{t-r-s}\sum_{k=0}^s\binom skx^k(1-x)^{s-k}dx .$$
The inner sum is $(x+(1-x))^s=1$ by the binomial theorem. Applying the lemma again with $t-s$ in place of $t$ (note $0\le r\le t-s$):
$$(t+1)\int_0^1x^r(1-x)^{(t-s)-r}dx=\frac{t+1}{(t-s+1)\binom{t-s}r}.$$
∎

putnam-1987-b2.title: Induction on s with Pascal's rule
putnam-1987-b2.body:
Let $L(r,s,t)$ denote the left side and $R(r,s,t)=\dfrac{t+1}{(t+1-s)\binom{t-s}r}$.

**Base $s=0$:** $L=\frac1{\binom tr}=R$.

**Key identity.** For $0\le r<N$:
$$\frac1{\binom Nr}+\frac1{\binom N{r+1}}=\frac{r!(N-r)!+(r+1)!(N-r-1)!}{N!}=\frac{r!(N-r-1)!\,(N+1)}{N!}=\frac{N+1}{N\binom{N-1}r}.$$

**Step.** Let $s\ge1$ and $r+s\le t$. By Pascal's rule $\binom sk=\binom{s-1}k+\binom{s-1}{k-1}$,
$$L(r,s,t)=L(r,s-1,t)+L(r+1,s-1,t),$$
and both terms satisfy the hypotheses ($r+1+s-1\le t$). By the induction hypothesis and the key identity with $N=t-s+1$ (note $r<N$),
$$L(r,s,t)=\frac{t+1}{t+2-s}\left(\frac1{\binom{t-s+1}r}+\frac1{\binom{t-s+1}{r+1}}\right)=\frac{t+1}{t+2-s}\cdot\frac{t-s+2}{(t-s+1)\binom{t-s}r}=R(r,s,t).$$
∎

putnam-1987-b3.title: Lines through the point (1,0)
putnam-1987-b3.body:
**The listed points are solutions.** $(1,0)$ clearly is. If $r^2\ne-1$ then
$$\left(\frac{r^2-1}{r^2+1}\right)^2+\left(\frac{2r}{r^2+1}\right)^2=\frac{r^4-2r^2+1+4r^2}{(r^2+1)^2}=\frac{(r^2+1)^2}{(r^2+1)^2}=1 .$$

**Every solution is listed.** Let $x^2+y^2=1$.

- If $x=1$, then $y^2=0$, so $y=0$: the point $(1,0)$.
- If $x\ne1$, put $r=\dfrac{y}{1-x}$, so $y=r(1-x)$. Substituting, $r^2(1-x)^2=1-x^2=(1-x)(1+x)$, and dividing by $1-x\ne0$:
$$r^2(1-x)=1+x,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad x(r^2+1)=r^2-1 .$$
If $r^2+1=0$, this says $0=r^2-1=-2$, impossible since $1+1\ne0$. So $r^2\ne-1$ and
$$x=\frac{r^2-1}{r^2+1},\qquad y=r(1-x)=r\cdot\frac{2}{r^2+1}=\frac{2r}{r^2+1}.$$

So the solution set is exactly $(1,0)$ together with the points of the given form. (Moreover the parametrization never produces $(1,0)$, since $\frac{r^2-1}{r^2+1}=1$ would mean $-1=1$, and different $r$ give different points, because $r=y/(1-x)$ is recovered from the point.) ∎

putnam-1987-b4.title: Polar coordinates
putnam-1987-b4.body:
**Rotation.** The recursion says $(x_{n+1},y_{n+1})$ is $(x_n,y_n)$ rotated about the origin by the angle $y_n$; in complex form $x_{n+1}+iy_{n+1}=e^{iy_n}(x_n+iy_n)$. Rotations preserve length, and $0.8^2+0.6^2=1$, so all points lie on the unit circle. Write
$$x_n=\cos\theta_n,\quad y_n=\sin\theta_n,\qquad \theta_1=\arcsin 0.6\in(0,\tfrac\pi2),\qquad \theta_{n+1}=\theta_n+\sin\theta_n .$$

**Behaviour of the angles.** Let $g(\theta)=\theta+\sin\theta$. For $0<\theta<\pi$:
- $g(\theta)>\theta$ since $\sin\theta>0$;
- $g(\theta)<\pi$, since $\sin\theta=\sin(\pi-\theta)<\pi-\theta$ (as $\sin u<u$ for $u>0$).

By induction $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\dots<\pi$. A bounded increasing sequence converges, say $\theta_n\to L\in(0,\pi]$. By continuity of $g$, $L=L+\sin L$, so $\sin L=0$, and $L\in(0,\pi]$ forces $L=\pi$.

**Conclusion.** By continuity of $\cos$ and $\sin$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n=\cos\pi=-1,\qquad\lim_{n\to\infty}y_n=\sin\pi=0 .$$
∎

putnam-1987-b5.title: Pass to a real 2n × 2n matrix
putnam-1987-b5.body:
Write $M=X+iY$ with $X,Y$ real $2n\times n$ matrices, and let $K=(X\mid Y)$ be the real $2n\times2n$ matrix whose first $n$ columns are those of $X$ and last $n$ columns those of $Y$.

**$K$ is invertible.** Let $z\in\mathbb R^{2n}$ be a real row vector with $zK=0$. Then $zX=0$ and $zY=0$, so $zM=zX+i\,zY=O_n$ with all $z_i$ real. By hypothesis this forces $z=0$. So $K$ has trivial left null space; being square, it is invertible. Changing the sign of the last $n$ columns preserves invertibility, so $K'=(X\mid -Y)$ is invertible too.

**Solving.** For $w=u+iv$ with $u,v\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$Mw=(X+iY)(u+iv)=(Xu-Yv)+i(Xv+Yu),\qquad\text{so}\qquad \mathrm{re}(Mw)=Xu-Yv=K'\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}.$$
Given any real $r=(r_1,\dots,r_{2n})^T$, let $\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}=K'^{-1}r$ and $w=u+iv$. Then $\mathrm{re}(Mw)=r$. ∎

putnam-1987-b6.title: Compare two products
putnam-1987-b6.body:
Let $m=|S|=\frac{p^2-1}2$. Since $p$ is odd, $2\ne0$ and $-1\ne1$ in $F$.

**A permutation of $S$.** For $a\in S$, $2a\ne0$, so exactly one of $2a,-2a$ lies in $S$; call it $\sigma(a)$. The map $\sigma:S\to S$ is injective: if $\sigma(a)=\sigma(a')$ then $2a=\pm2a'$, so $a=\pm a'$, and since $S$ never contains both $c$ and $-c$, $a=a'$. Hence $\sigma$ is a bijection of the finite set $S$.

Note $\sigma(a)=2a$ exactly when $2a\in S$, i.e. for exactly $N$ elements $a\in S$ (the elements $2a\in S\cap 2S$ correspond bijectively to these $a$). For the other $m-N$ elements, $\sigma(a)=-2a$.

**Products.** Let $\Pi=\prod_{a\in S}a\ne0$. Since $\sigma$ is a bijection,
$$\Pi=\prod_{a\in S}\sigma(a)=(-1)^{m-N}\,2^m\,\Pi,\qquad\text{so}\qquad (-1)^{m-N}2^m=1 .$$

**$2^m=1$.** $2$ lies in the prime field $\mathbb F_p$, so $2^{p-1}=1$ (Fermat). Since $m=(p-1)\cdot\frac{p+1}2$ and $\frac{p+1}2$ is an integer, $2^m=1$.

**Conclusion.** Thus $(-1)^{m-N}=1$, and as $-1\ne1$ in $F$, $m-N$ is even. Finally $m=\frac{(p-1)(p+1)}2$ is even, because $(p-1)(p+1)$ is a product of two consecutive even numbers, hence divisible by $8$. Therefore $N$ is even. ∎
